She suggests where to place certain pieces of furniture and gives her view on some questions about the work to be done. She wants news of the Father and to know whether Vincenza has been to the Vicar to have the letter about him written. Anna wants the stockings.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received yours acknowledging my unstamped letter, in which you go to such pains to convince me of what I was already more than convinced of, and there was no need even to tell that person, since you put a wrapper on it and that was that. Can you still doubt and think I might suppose you could ever betray me? Naughty girl!1

2. Listen, now to the work. You ask about having it painted and say the whole corridor will cost F. 50; well, it's better to spend it; it's necessary, so it must be done; God will see to it; have it painted.

3. So listen: the wardrobes in the corridor — you know, the three black ones — I'd like you to remove them, because they look bad in corridors; put one, the one half full of cloth and half of Carlotta's dresses, in your room; the other two downstairs, one in the room where we work, where the big chest of drawers is, and the other big one where the blankets go in the lamp room, where you're having the marble basin put; and the sofa there, out with it too, put it downstairs in the parlour; in short, the main corridor as far as St Francis must be empty. Those two gilt ones,2 leave them where they are, for they look well.

4. I've written yes to painting the door. If you see that the tracetta curtains3 are needed, have them made. I'd like the builders to finish the upstairs rooms quickly; the kitchen whitewash can wait; we'll have it done when things are further on.

5. I'd like you to try to keep few girls and send them all to Poss, so that there are as few as possible in the house.

6. You don't mention that person any more, and from the way you write I think you've had a row, haven't you? What happened? write and tell me. I hope you've received mine telling you to go to the Vicar and ask him to tell the Bishop too, provided he writes it well and not like last year's; you can tell that person so.4

7. I've arranged the opening of another house in Perugia, and we'll go there when I come down. I'm held captive here and don't know what to do. One fine day I'll just leave everything and come away. I'm tired.

8. Listen, about Signora Iussi's girl,5 note that she has sent me F. 100 once and for all and wants her to go into the factory; this for your guidance. I'd like all the good ones to go there; I'm waiting for the letter to see whether I get anywhere, and then I'll come away.6

9. I'm much better; but I always keep a blister open and find it does me good; when one comes off I put on another.7

Goodbye, yours for all ages,

affectionate M.; and you ever my dearest and most beloved daughter-sister above all others

10. Anna wants you to send her some stockings. Listen, see whether there are any new ones among Augusta's, and if you have a chance send them; if not, write that there are some but you're waiting for an opportunity, and try to string it out.8 I've given her mine for now, so she can manage for a while. Dear Vincenza, the cotton you sent her is too fine; it takes too long to knit and besides it's too dainty for Daughters of Saint Anne. If you had some thicker, even dark, she'd take it; but don't trouble to buy it or send things, for it costs too much and isn't worth it.

11. Goodbye again, yours, yours; keep well, for charity's sake, so we can still work.

12. How it pleases me when you tell me what you've done

in the house! Put the postulant9 in the rooms I wrote to you about, which will be for the Noviciate, in a bed with its curtains.

1 Sr. A. Vincenza had absent-mindedly opened a letter of the Mother's en-

closed in hers, but realizing it was for Fr Tornatore, without reading it she had

hastened to put it in an envelope and explain to the Father what had happened.

2 Those two: the two gilt sofas.

3 Curtains of non-transparent fabric, Sr. A. Vincenza wrote.

4 That person: Fr Tornatore. Had there been a clash? You'll have received

mine. The letter is missing, but there is Sr. A. Vincenza's reply (7 April), in which she

describes at length her meeting with the Bishop's Vicar, Mgr Francesco

Tammi, to ask him for a letter to send to Rome to obtain Fr Tornatore's

readmission to the Institute.

5 Signora Clotilde Iussi helped several girls staying at the Mother House.

6 This is the letter from Vicar Tammi mentioned in note 4 above.

7 a mosca: a blister.

8 Anna Carrega; Sr. A. Augusta Biagini's.

9 The postulant from Rome. Cf. L 237, n. 4.

The postulant will come at the end of the month, and the Mother hopes she will find everything in order. Poss has written complaining that the Sister in charge of the girls is absent; Vincenza is to go there and urge them to behave well. For the Chapel's inauguration she wants the ceremony to go well: spare no expense, invite many Priests. She hopes there are sheets in the wardrobe and that many are brought: she needs them for all the houses.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I received yours yesterday and hear you're unwell; for charity's sake take care of yourself; write to me, for I'm worried; I'm better and we'll soon see each other.

2. Yes, have the cloth you mention dyed. I'd like it done soon, so that when this postulant comes she may find everything in order: the marble basins, the wardrobes moved and the Novices' beds ready, and put her in one of them; she'll come at the end of the month, leaving with me; I'll stop at Foligno and she'll go on.1

3. Poss wrote complaining that Sr. A. Buon Pastore is in bed, so all the girls seem to be at sixes and sevens. For charity's sake try to go there and urge the girls to be good; if you think more Religious are needed, go ahead, I'm content, as long as it goes well.2

4. I want the ceremony to be done without any stinting: breakfast for the Vicar, and the two F. for the servers and clerics. Tell Don Piacenza to spare nothing, for whatever

is needed will be paid. I'd like there to be many Priests; invite the Superior of S. Lazzaro. Make sure there are Priests: our Canon and whoever you think.3

5. I hear about the butcher; how dreadful! Let's hope in God; we'll have everything; I can't wait to hear about the letter sent.4

6. As for the harmonium, you answered well; stick to it that it's too big and always gets damaged when moved, and that he'll do us a great favour by lending his; tell him that if he thinks maestro Volpi should be engaged, you'll engage him. Mind you decorate the Chapel well. As for the pyx, you can ask Don Piacenza to buy you one,5 you know, one of the composite ones I know they have in Piacenza; or else I'll write — never mind, I'll write to Sr. A. Santina to send you one, so there'll be no more muddle. What is that person doing — has he been to the Vicar?

7. You tell me there's no more room in the wardrobe for cloth; I'd be only too happy if it were full, but I fear it's [full] on only two shelves and the other two hold the sheets, of which I hope there's a good number. If it were so, let it fill up; then you could put the sheets in the one where the postulants' dresses are and fold those all into a chest, which will be better. Ah, would to God lots of sheets came, for I need them for all the houses. See, my dear, for charity's sake don't pass them on to the girls.6

8. Take care of yourself; write at once to tell me how you are. Goodbye,

yours for ever,

Affectionate [MADRE ROSA]

9. This is the third time I've taken this up again. I write as I talk.

Goodbye, my dear; be cheerful, for charity's sake; please tell the Supe-

rior at the Morte to be at peace and that there's nothing wrong;

patience is needed.7

1 This Postulant, cf. L 237, n. 4.

2 Sr. A. del Buon Pastore Dosi was in bed. Someone was needed to replace her,

and other Sisters too.

3 The inauguration ceremony for the Poss factory chapel was to be

held on Low Sunday, 12 April. On 7 April Sr. A. Vincenza had asked her for

clarifications and all the permissions. The Mother replies in detail. The two F.

(francs) to be given to the two clerics and the master of ceremonies. The Superior of S. Lazzaro,

i.e. of the Alberoni College. Our Canon: no further information about him.

4 I hear about the butcher: he had surely complained about late pay-

ment. On 13 April Sr. A. Vincenza writes: "Pastore (Sr. A. Buon Pastore) told me there's a debt of Fr. 400 and the miller won't give us flour; for now I have only a few francs." But the Mother does not lose trust in God, either for providence or for Fr Tornatore's readmission to the Institute. That is what she refers to here: I can't wait to hear about the letter sent. It is the request from Bishop Ranza obtained by Sr. A. Vincenza. Cf. L 241, n. 4 and below, par. 6: has that Person been to the Vicar?

5 As for the harmonium. Sr. A. Vincenza's letter is missing and it cannot

be learned from any other source what was said, and by whom, about the harmonium for the inaugu-

ration of the chapel. Don Pietro Piacenza, chaplain of the Mother House.

6 You tell me there's no more room in the wardrobe for the linen

cloth; I'd be only too happy if it were full. The Mother thinks there is no room

girls: the linen belonged to the Community, having been brought for the most

part by postulants who had joined the Institute.

7 The Superior of the Community in Via della Morte: Sr. A. Filippina Bruschi.

As for the Chaplain for the Sampierdarena Community, she should speak with Don Accinelli; the Mother proposes a plan: he could be lodged in a room in the tenant farmer's house and take meals in the Sisters' house. After the clothing she is to send two novices to Genoa, and the others must leave. When Don Accinelli comes to Rome the Mother can settle the matter of the Chaplain with him.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Today I received your letter, so dear to me; the good news you give me is a relief amid so many bitter things [all] day long; my breathing still isn't free; I can't understand it, though I always keep the blisters open; nothing helps. Enough, I hope I'll recover when I leave.1

2. As for the priest, you'd do well to speak with Don Accinelli, as this is a very delicate matter, requiring careful enquiries; I don't know where they could put him; anyway, I want it arranged; another 100 F. or so could be added for lodging, so he wouldn't always be a cross for the nuns.2 Tell Don Accinelli, to whom I'm writing now. If it could be arranged it would be good all round; see what you can do.

3. I hear the seven postulants are being clothed; I hope all goes well; the teacher, in strict confidence, is to serve me for the new house we're going to open in Perugia; silence, for charity's sake; in a few days the one for Sestri will reach you; you'll see her; she seems well suited to me.3

4. Otherwise everything you're doing is fine; you say in one of your letters you want to laugh; as I write, what I had to tell you comes back (to) mind; it's really odd, my dear, when one has to deal with certain creatures who make my head spin; you understand me, don't you? My head can't take it, from every side.4

5. Now, once those 7 are clothed, you'll send them to Genoa; try to leave only (che) the two teachers there and send all the others away, for that house carries too heavy a burden. Ah, when will the holy Mother think of relieving us of those two heartless ones? Enough; I hope the good God will see to it.5

6. Please try to settle the matter of the Priest, if possible; I'd prefer him not to sleep there; eat, yes, but sleep, no. Since at the end of the Villa there's the tenant farmer's house, which is big, perhaps a room could be fitted up there, giving the farmer the ground floor where the brothers still keep timber, and making one upstairs for the Priest with a separate little staircase. What do you think of my plan?6

7. Let Don Accinelli know of it, but without showing him the letter; indeed try to tell him that if you can help in any way he should tell you and you'll do it. Meanwhile hurry things along and try to visit the place together, so you could very well settle things with the Priest, and at last all the gossip would end; and since Don Accinelli comes to Rome on Monday, on his return — so he could tell the Priest — everything would be settled.7

Goodbye, my dear daughter; the Lord give you peace of heart; and always, for all ages, your

affectionate M.

1 Sr. A. Francesca's letter has not survived. My breathing...

cf. L 241,9.

2 As for the priest to be engaged as chaplain at the Sampier-

darena Institute: she doesn't know where they could put him, i.e. lodge him; the cost of

lodging outside could be reckoned, so he would not be a burden (cross) to the Sisters.

3 House in Perugia: cf. L 241,7. The one: the teacher for Sestri.

4 troubles and worries on every side.

5 too heavy a burden, maintaining so many people: ...the two heartless

ones, the Vernengo Sisters. Every day they showed little love for the Community

by their demands. Cf. L 206, n. 5.

6 Since at the end of the villa: a solution for lodging the Priest

occurs to her.

7 hurry things along: try to speed it up. Accinelli is coming to Rome to attend

The postulant can be admitted only on two conditions: that she give up the tobacco habit and submit to a period of probation at the Mother House. As for the other one sent to Piacenza, the Mother points out that she did not keep to what had been laid down about the fee to be paid.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to answer your letter and also the request of the postulant you have with you. With the tobacco habit she can't be admitted; it's forbidden by our Rules; secondly, she would have to go and make her postulancy in Piacenza, since it has been decided that no one may be clothed unless first well tested at the Mother House: they must give sure proof of obedience, vocation and submission.1

2. If she submits to all this, let her find the money for the journey and go to Piacenza with a letter from you — provided she gives up tobacco.

3. I was taken aback by the old woman you sent to Piacenza with so little, when you'd written she'd have much more. It's done now, but don't let it happen again, for so old and with nothing... They're just furniture cluttering our poor house.2

4. I, thanks [to] God, am a little better and trust in

your prayers to obtain all I desire for the work. Goodbye, your

Affectionate M.

1 The postulant claimed she took snuff as a medicine.

2 of the old postulant (cf. L 225,1 and 240,1): contrary to what

she had previously claimed, she had brought very little money (the two postulants

together had given L. 187). Furniture: i.e. encumbrances for our poor house.

She did not write sooner because she was waiting for the Bishop's reply about the two Sisters she wanted to send. Carlotta is to visit the Bishop to find out whether the proposal displeased him. The Mother hopes to be in Pennabilli in mid-May.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Some days ago I received yours together with one from Sr. A. Adelaide; I was slow to reply because I was waiting for a letter from the Bishop answering one I'd written telling him that if it's because of the journey that they don't call the Sisters, I would pay for it. What do you think? Perhaps the Bishop didn't (le) like this? Listen, go and pay him a visit and find out a little.1

2. I hope to be with you by mid-May, so we can settle everything properly in person and spend a little time together.

3. My dear daughter, courage, for great is the crown the good God has prepared for you if you always persevere as you do.

Greet everyone for me. I wish them a thousand blessings from heaven, while you, my beloved daughter, I hug tightly, remaining for ever your

affectionate M. R.

1 Sr. A. Carlotta replies to this letter on 19.4. She has been to the Bishop. He is "very troubled at not having been able to answer you... he did all he could with the President too, but could obtain nothing". She approves all Vincenza has planned and done to arrange the rooms. To increase the number of girls working at Poss she can approach various people. The Mother is troubled about the cash dowry postulants must bring: if little is asked, or they are accepted free, how can they be maintained? She asks about the dormitories and suggests some additions.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just received yours and am replying; I hope you've received mine urging you to speak to that person so that he wouldn't stir a straw; if he hasn't done it, let him not do it now; he should have gone earlier.1

2. You did well about the sheets; for charity's sake see that all who come bring at least a good quantity, so we can build up a large stock; for you know I've accepted another house in Perugia and I have to provide all the linen; so see to it, my dear.2

3. I'm glad to hear all the work is finished; now I'm waiting to hear the upstairs is done; as they finish the rooms, put them in order, so they'll be ready for the postulants at once.

4. We'll find the girls I promised Poss here and there; I think the Parish Priest of the Paganina still has some; look into it; I hear you've taken two more, so that'll be 18, not twenty. If Accinelli has some, you can write asking him to send them, or tell Sr. A. Francesca. Listen, send her a portrait, poor thing; I'm writing to her now.3

5. How it grieves me to hear we could have had money for that postulant and instead only 200 F. How dreadful! My dear, God knows how much we need; stand firm when they come with that line; tell them: "we can't!" He won't have thought of it; and hold firm at F. 500.4 I've accepted another one here, but for F. 800, if she comes. I hope you'll do it; so if he said it, we say so too; it certainly is a serious matter. Who pays the three hundred francs for meat? and we can never put a cent together. How this house grieves me, the more so now that there are more mouths.5

6. Find out what the baths are called that Mother Landi goes to every year; she'd like to know what they're good for. If you see Albertazzi you can ask him. Listen, it occurs to me that Albertazzi is owed F. 200 for 1873.6

7. And you can't imagine how the chemist's bill worries me; never mind the Marchioness!7 My dear, if we wait for help from her, I think the Daughters of Saint Anne would starve. Isn't that so, my Vincenza?

8. If you thought of making a trip to Cortemaggiore to fetch the postulant before I send the one from Rome, you wouldn't have to move again; meanwhile you'd pay; between the two you'd settle all the bills.8

9. I've started praying again for that house, and I hope the funds will reach you and you'll soon write to tell me.

10. How is your room? And is ours finished? When will you clothe the ones I wrote to you about? And when are you putting Cecilia at the end of the Novices' dormitory?9 But I'd like her not to make a mess; keep it clean.

11. Have you had any iron frames made for the beds in the girls' dormitory that's closed? What would you say if we managed to put frames on every other bed, with curtains: what luxury! Then girls of every kind could go there, couldn't they?10

12. But if postulants keep coming with nothing, it's dreadful! Expenses on every side and never any income! I commend the sheets to you.

13. Now the things you want to send: I'd say send nothing; they'd like salami, but what can I say, transport costs too much, and for so few days; it seems a waste of money. Goodbye, yours for an eternity.

Affectionate M.

14. P.S. Silence: on Monday that person takes the veil; pray and have others pray; tell that person; it's a tremendous business.11

She tells her that Anna's Clothing will take place the next day. Don Gaetano has written wanting to be paid by Don Biale; Vincenza is to speak to Don Biale and urge him to pay his debts, borrowing from Don Accinelli. She asks for some information and urges her to look after her health and live in peace.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Read this letter to C. and then give it to Mr T. to read; imagine, you know I never had any thought of accepting such creatures; nor does Mr Poss want them, you know, because they're lazy. Enough; Piacenza always has something new. Now I'm writing to Poss and to the Bishop so that he can answer these most worthy Sisters.1

2. My dear, tomorrow Anna's clothing takes place. Imagine what battles (che) will arise, but let's pay no heed; courage; until death we'll cry: "Long live Jesus!"2 I can't wait to leave Rome. I'm tired; I hope you've received my letter.

3. Listen: Don Gaetano writes that he wants to be paid by Don Biale; do me the kindness of going there and telling him, for charity's sake, to pay these people, and the doctor too; let him write to Don Accinelli to lend him the money, but let him pay. If he writes like that, Accinelli will send it; so let him not put it off any longer.3

4. Ah, I'd also like you to be able to pay the doctor for 1873.4 Let's hope the Lord sends you the money. My expenses here are an abyss.

5. When you see my dear postulant, I'm sure you'll be pleased.5 Today I thought I'd get letters from you, lazybones! I write to you every day. Tomorrow is the great ceremony.

6. And then that person hasn't gone again to commend himself? What patience! My dear, everything falls on the one with the flayed back: everything on me!6

7. When convenient, I'd like you to write and tell me how many sheets there are — you know, only those belonging strictly to the community, not those the postulants brought; forgive my curiosity; it will guide me when I ask you for some.

8. For charity's sake don't overtire yourself; take care; do what you do in peace; keep after the gardener too, so he works the garden well and puts it in good order.

9. Tell me, do you know anything more about the Marchioness?7 They've written to me that all is at peace. Blessed be the Lord!

10. Goodbye, for I still have so much to write. Your affectionate M.

for ever, and always near, to enjoy the sufferings we have

borne. Yes, my dear, what consolation! we'll laugh at everyone and

live with Jesus for eternity. Long live suffering!8

your Affectionate M. R.

3 Don Gaetano Bersani and the doctor wanted to be paid by Don Biale

6 That person: Fr Tornatore was to commend himself; to whom, we cannot

know.

7 Marchioness Fanny Anguissola, cf. L 100, n. 10.

8 Suffering makes us long for, and prepares us for, eternal joy, where no one can make us suffer any more; we shall live with Jesus for ever.

She thanks her for what she sent through Alessandro. Her news of the house is a joy, but even more what she says about keeping the Rules. She is glad they are at last in a bigger house. She urges them to love the Lord; in pleasing him one is happy and gives true witness.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Forgive me for not writing as soon as I received the decoction; it was the great pressure of work. Now I'm with you to say how welcome the decoction was and how much good it did me; one bottle broke, a pity;1 there was a big stone in the basket, it must have been that; thank you also for the orange-flower water.

2. My daughter, how your letters please me, always bringing such consoling news of providence and of the house;2 but what pleases me most is when you tell me the Rules are kept, and when I hear you have many sick people.

3. Now that the house is bigger I'll send you nurses, so you can do more nursing without wearing yourselves out; that's my wish.3

4. Courage, my daughter, and pray for me, for the tribulations are immense; I desire nothing but to bear them with resignation and as my God wills! Yes, my dear, when I can be sure that what I do and suffer pleases my Jesus, I am happy; so I hope of you and the others that your happiness will be nothing other than pleasing the Lord.4

Yes! once we have attained this, my dears, we want nothing more.

5. Enough! enough! Love dear Jesus very much and then be cheerful, so as to make everyone want to follow you in the apostolate of converting souls.5 Courage, for one day we shall rest for eternity.

Your Affectionate M. God bless you all. Pray, pray!

1 Cf. L 239, n. 2.

2 news... of the house, cf. L 239, n. 3.

3 The sick wanting to be nursed by the Sisters were always numerous.

4 your happiness... pleasing the Lord. This sums up her trinitarian spiri-

tuality: guided by the Spirit, with Jesus and in Jesus, to be the delight of the

Father.

5 Love and be cheerful: to witness by one's life how beautiful and joyful it is

to live for Jesus is the most effective apostolate for attracting souls.

?

From the Parrocchietta she gives the good news of Anna Carrega's Clothing; she is now Sr. A. Benedetta. She suggests Francesca advise Sr. A. Santina to send her some money. She wants the Sisters to lack nothing: they work and need enough food. She is to do her best to have the Communities follow the Spiritual Exercises preached by Fr Defilippi.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I'm at the Parrocchietta and, having a little time, I'm giving part of it to you, my dear, whom I always keep with me wherever I go. Do you know why I'm here? enough, I'll tell you in person, for fear this gets lost.

2. Now I've good news for you: Anna is ours; since yesterday (che) she's been called Sr. A. Benedetta. Silence, silence, for charity's sake!1

3. I hope they'll bring me letters from you today, but I'm going down at once, not stopping, and I hope (che) to leave early in May; you know we've opened another house in Perugia.2

4. Listen, now that Don Accinelli is away, I'd like you (che) to tell Sr. A. Santina — as if from yourself — to set aside the money she receives and then send it to me, I mean a month's worth, after expenses, and to pay for the flour herself, so she gets used to managing on her own. What do you think? Listen, I'm suggesting this, but do it only if you think fit. Think it over and then do as you judge best. I don't say they should give him nothing, but a third, which would be somewhat more than the rent;3 tell

her to feed the Sisters well, and that the bread be good. That's my wish. Since providence is coming in there, let them lack nothing; waste, no — against the dear jewel of poverty, no — but too little and poor food, no either, for they work very hard.4

5. I hope you've seen to the Chapel. I can't wait to hear you announce it.5 I hope Defilippi will also give the Exercises at S. P. d'Arena in the house, and then to you in the hospital; do them as best you can; that's my wish; and at Sestri too; make the most of it. At Sestri see that they prepare a nicely arranged room for him, and let him go there too, so I won't have to think about it for a year.6

6. I rely on you. I very much hope he'll take those two vipers in hand and straighten out their heads; it would be a first-class miracle. I'm writing him a couple of lines now to encourage him to do what is so badly needed.7

7. Have you perhaps had Carlotta's dress made? Then you could send it to her, for she'd take off her heavy wool, as it's already warm.8

8. I hope you've thought about the Priest and received my letter.9 This time I hope you won't complain that I write too little. I'm always in credit. Ah, my dear Francesca, one day indeed we shall no longer need to write or long for news of each other, but held close together we shall be with our Good, to enjoy him for eternity. Then all our pains will seem little to us, seeing that they alone brought us a great good. Courage! Long live the cross with suffering! Long may it live!10

Yours for ever,

affectionate M. R.

2 I'm going down: back to Rome. We've opened another house in Perugia: that

3 Now he's away: Don Accinelli was in Rome. He managed the

Genoa house, and the Superior Santina handed him the surplus money.

Now the Mother wants the Superior to get used to managing herself, but leaves it to the

discretion of Sr. A. Francesca. I don't say they should give nothing to Don Acci-

nelli, but a third of the surplus, so that he can pay the rent and

some other expenses.

4 Let her feed them well... for they work very hard. Cf. L 135,6; 136,5; 138, n. 7; 175,6.

6 Giuseppe Defilippi was to preach the Spiritual Exercises to the Community.

Cf. L 206,9.

7 I hope he'll take in hand: that he'll manage to bring the two Ver-

8 Carlotta's dress; the Mother had asked her for it. Cf. L 218,5.

9 the priest: the chaplain for the Sampierdarena House. Cf. L 243,2,6,7.

10 To her dear daughter, who longs to have her near, she opens the vision of an inex-

pressible joy, free of anxiety and waiting, the fulfilment of a joy unattainable on

earth — a joy all the more intense the more numerous the

sufferings have been. Courage! Forward with zeal under the banner of the cross.

Thinking again about what she advised in the previous letter, she asks her not to speak to the Superior Santina about the financial matter in question.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to tell you that for charity's sake you must say nothing to Sr. A. Santina, for it would be a serious matter; if you've already spoken to her, try to go there and put it right, telling her to take no notice whatever of what you said.2

2. Sleep is overcoming me; it's late and today I'm very tired. You can imagine I have Don Accinelli with me.3 Enough, I'm going to sleep. I'll tell you everything in person.

I am your affectionate MADRE

1 This letter was sent after the previous one (cf. L 249).

2 Contrary to what she had advised her to suggest to the Supe-

rior Santina, after speaking with Don Accinelli she has understood that it is better not

to change anything (cf. L 249,4).

3 He had come to Rome for Anna Carrega's clothing.

She is to keep the sick girl at the Mother House. She is to clothe the postulants, but after the Spiritual Exercises. She is to finish the work on the house and pay the debts. The Mother longs to leave Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I haven't written for two days because of the heavy work that doesn't leave me a minute. In your last you told me Sireni is ill; for pity's sake don't send her there again; take her home with you.1

2. You told me you have postulants to clothe; I say yes, but first I'd like them to make at least 5 days' retreat; then clothe them as soon as you can, for they're needed.

3. I hope the builders will soon finish upstairs; while they're there, we'll have to do the laundry. Did you have the corridor shutters cleaned, which you said needed it — I don't remember — and I wrote yes? Be quick and pay all the bills, for charity's sake, so they can't say anything more.

4. Go and see Marchioness Anguissola; if only the Lord would touch her heart!2

5. Yesterday I went to the Pope and had a private audience. What fine things he said to me! Next Thursday we're going to the Fornaci with Mgr Negrotto, and then, if they finish the Father's business, I'll leave at once.3

6. I'm waiting for letters from you; that person must be always asleep, for he no longer writes.4 I can't wait to leave. My

health is good; I get up early, I work — crippled, yes, but always on my feet. God be blessed! I owe it all to my Rosa, dear holy creature.5 [Nothing] more for now, as I have to go out. Yours for ever,

affectionate M. R.

2 Marchioness Anguissola. Cf. L 100, n. 10.

n. 4; 242, n. 4.

4 Fr Tornatore.

5 My Rosa Parodi, the dear friend who died in the odour of sanctity, to whom

she prayed with confidence and whose powerful interces-

sion she felt. Cf. L 178, n. 1.

She outlines her travel plans. Notes on the postulants and their accommodation. Vincenza is to send Carlotta, who will travel with Don Accinelli, her half-mourning dress.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've just finished reading your letter about D. Giovanni. You did well in what you write; now D. Accinelli will come and give him what he deserves; meanwhile be patient.1

2. As for the postulants, for charity's sake clothe as many as you can, lots of them, for I need them desperately. Instead of one from Rome I'm sending you 2, very good ones. On Saturday I leave for Foligno, where I'll stay 5 or 6 days, then Perugia for 2 days, then Pennabilli, Bologna, Ferrara and Piacenza at last.

3. Please see to the washbasins; rest assured I'll be pleased with whatever you've done.2

4. Put the postulant who's coming with the young Lady — she too is a young lady — wherever you think best, as long as it's suitable and clean. As for the lame postulant, you can tell him to send her for you to see, and if you can take her, take her. The other two, if they're strong, accept them, for charity's sake, even with F. 100, simply because I need them; and as you clothe those you have, others will come at once. It stays always full.3

5. Now listen: you told me you've had iron frames4 fitted to four of the girls' beds in the big dormitory; well done; but I'd also like you to arrange these four beds like this: right at the top by the door one with curtains, then

one without, then one with curtains and one without — that's four; you have two left over, so put them on the other side as you come in, one with and one without, and in the curtained ones you can put the young ladies. All right? That's for when you have no more room to put them. What do you think? For washing, let them always go where the girls used to go. Since they're nuns, I think they'll be able to keep it clean there, and they could draw water from the well, putting on top, if you think fit, that container with a tap that was in the girls' kitchen; it could be set a little into the wall and fixed. What do you think? It would look good in marble, but for now we must economize; in due course; meanwhile they could keep this one always full, and so they'd all wash there.

6. Try to have a few pictures made to put in

those rooms the builders are fixing up. I hear you have no

money; I hope that today St Joseph, it being his Patronage, will have

sent you some.5 Goodbye, yours for all ages,

M. affectionate

7. Carlotta asks you to send her the half-mourning dress she has in the wardrobe, last year's grey one, because she needs it for the journey right away. She's staying in Rome while I go to Foligno. Don Accinelli will bring it to me;6 send it at once; it will arrive in time; don't delay a moment once you've received this. Send me nothing else. Goodbye; everyone sends greetings.

8. As for bread, you can give it to the girls with a little slice of fat bacon, and they'd be happy.7

a soup, they could put the bit of bread left over in their pockets and

She gives instructions about the Sister nurses attending Signora Airenta.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line to tell you to go and visit Signora Airenta at S. P. d'Arena1 and tell her that if she needs nurses I've written to you to send her two for a week, and after that week they'll be changed for another two.

2. They'll stay there day and night and eat what the Lady gives them — you know, two dishes and soup and a piece of fruit; do it at once. Send Emanuela and one of the most recently clothed;2 for the next week send another two. I'm writing to Piacenza to send you two at once.

Goodbye, in haste, your

Affectionate M.

1 Signora Paola Airenta, her friend and a benefactress of the Institute.

2 Sr. A. Emanuela Zumi, older in vocation.

She has told the Superiors to send the post to Piacenza. Until the 7th she will be in Foligno and will tell her where and when to forward it. She has had a letter from the Father and is pleased with what has been done at the Poss factory. She has obtained the Holy Father's blessing for it.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. For your guidance: on Saturday, God willing, I leave for Foligno; if you receive letters from other Superiors — as I've written to them all to send them to you there — you'll always know my movements. She announces her imminent departure and asks that letters be addressed to Piacenza. The Superior is to pray and have prayers said for her long journey.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. A line in haste to tell you I leave Rome on Saturday 2 May. Address your letters to Piacenza, where they have orders to forward them to me wherever I am.1

2. I've received yours and heard all about the Countess, and about the Schools.2

3. Have prayers said that I may have a good journey, for it's very long and tiring; pray to the most blessed Virgin that nothing may happen to me and that I may arrive safely.

Goodbye; greet everyone for me. God bless you, and believe me your

affectionate M. ROSA

She has received her letter. She will write later to let her know where she is. Vincenza is to write the address and hand letters to the postman. Her letter brought consolation with the news that every debt is paid. She commends to her the two postulants arriving from Rome.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. Yesterday I received your letter and two lines from that person. At last the decision has gone out; by now you'll know everything; I'm told the favour has been granted; write at once to tell me how it was done, and tell me everything properly, for you know Fr S. never says things clearly; so I'm waiting to hear it from you.2 Meanwhile I'm going to thank Our Lady of Loreto.

affec[tionate]

She received her letter a few hours ago and leaves for Foligno today. She has explained to D. Accinelli what Vincenza wanted to know about the work. She is pleased with what she is doing; she should not worry about the girls: they will recover.

My daughter,

She thanks her for the money order and asks for prayers.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your letter with the money order inside. Thank you for remembering and for your good heart towards your poor mother; I didn't write sooner because I received it the very moment I was leaving,2 and then on arrival you know how busy I am.

2. Tell the Sisters to pray hard for the journey I have to make,3 and that I may complete all I told them before leaving. Goodbye, for I'm in a hurry; your

Affectionate Mother

1 It was classified as dated 6 April 1874, from Rome. The content shows

She warmly urges observance, without which the service of charity is reduced to mere human labour, lacking the foundation of faith and charity. She is unwell and longs to be with her daughters. She hopes to see her again in Piacenza. Francesca is to look after herself and get treatment.

A.M.F.

My daughter,

1. I've received your long letter telling me so much about observance.1 My daughter, listen: if you don't see to it that it is kept, everything else will go from bad to worse. Observance is the pivot of our actions; without it we can do no good; laxity sets in, harmony among the Sisters vanishes, grumbling becomes the main business of the day, and worse, certain ugly things follow which are the ruin of communities. Observance is the sweet bond of perfection, which helps us one another to run along that dear path of peace and union.2

2. For pity's sake, try to put things in order, otherwise it's merely human labour and will end with the fall of our life; let us build on solid ground, not on sand, so that our buildings may last for eternity.3

3. Those two Sisters, so stubborn and proud — punish them without pity; death is better than living out of God's grace; pride is abhorred by Jesus, so whoever is proud is sure to be abhorred by the Lord and can expect nothing but eternal death.4

4. Listen, I hope to be in Piacenza on Saturday, because I don't feel well, so I'm hurrying the journey out of fear. Today I'm breathing

better, but yesterday I had to apply a blister; I can't wait to be in your arms. How I miss you! Well, you spoiled me, so it's hard to be away from you. I remember all the things you did for me. Ah, you spoiled me far too much!5

5. Enough; see whether you can arrange with the director to have two days' leave: I'd telegraph you, but I don't know how. What can I say, at stations I have to do everything myself, so — what a trial — I feel ill having to do one thing after another; I don't know whether I'll manage. Anyway, you know, don't you? So unless you have some objection, on Saturday next week I'll be in Piacenza. Goodbye. Take care of yourself, for charity's sake; look after your health, for once lost it can't be regained. Goodbye, for my side hurts. God bless you with the others; your

affectionate M. R. I leave here on Monday, the day after tomorrow.6

1 Sr. A. Francesca's letter is of 2 May. The hospital work certainly kept the Sisters busy full time and made community acts difficult and sometimes impossible.

2 If you don't see to it that it is kept. In a few lines the Mother

encapsulates great wisdom. Observance of the Rule is the pivot of

action because it fills it with charity towards God and the sick. Observance attunes

the Sisters to one rhythm and is a source of peace, harmony and mutual

agreement, leading all to unity.

3 The conclusion is full of the Gospel spirit: build on rock, not

on sand, otherwise our life will be fruitless in time and in eternity.

Cf. Matt 7:24-27.

4 Those two stubborn and proud Sisters. They must be corrected for their own good. The

proud person runs not on the way towards Jesus but on the way away

from him, the way of death.

5 to be there on Saturday. Instead she went to Rimini. Cf. L 261. I can't wait: a frank

and spontaneous outpouring of affectionate gratitude and tenderness towards the Daughters

who had surrounded her with attention and tenderness.

6 I leave here on Monday the 11th. She actually left on Wednesday the 13th.

I'd better telegraph you when I leave Bologna, so you'll know my arrival in Piacenza more surely.

Goodbye; I'm sorry to hear you haven't received letters from me; it means they're getting lost. Patience!

Goodbye, your

affectionate M.

My daughter,

Le scrive da Invorio Inferiore, dove dovrà impiantare una comunità, faccia partire perciò le Sorelle Paola e Gesuina. Le chiede di spedire la copia dei permessi concessi per le Cappelle dell'Istituto.

A.M.F. Figliola mia,

1. Da ieri sera che sono arrivata in questo paese del Lago Maggiore. Avrai ricevuto il mio telegramma e ne attendo le religiose, due: Paola e Gesuina, perché le altre le prenderò in altri siti.1 Tu sarai stata in pena perché non avrai mie lettere.

2. Dopo un viaggio assai curioso e di non poco strapazzo giunsimo ieri sera alle 9J al nostro destino, questo paese si chiama Invorio Inferiore; ci sono due ore di vettura, ma noi ne feci-mo quattro, perché andammo dal Vicario, oggi poi ne farò altre due ore per andare dal Vescovo Mons. Gentile.2

3. Senti, mandami subito le carte, ossia la copia del permesso delle Cappelle, tutti i permessi che abbiamo, ricopiali e mandali a questo indirizzo: Boffetti Giovanni Parroco di Ve-spolate.3

4. Noialtre siamo [a] Invorio Inferiore, non mi stare a scrivere perché spero venerdì di partire, andare ad Ovada dove giungerò alla notte.4 Oh! dove siamo mio Dio! Avvisa quella persona che non mi scriva sino che non ha mie lettere, che sia ferma. Ad-

dio. Carlotta sarà partita? Mi sembra cento lettere.

Sono alla fine del mondo, tua in fretta

anni di non vedere

Aff. M. R.

1 Sr. A. Paola Bucciotti e Sr. A. Gesuina Moroni.

2 Mons. Giacomo Gentile, Vescovo di Novara.

L 160). Il Parroco di Vespolate (Prov. di Novara), è D. Giovanni Boffetti. Cf.

4 Venerdì, 17.

5 Si sarà recata a Genova? (cf. L 315,4; 318,7).
